# Summary: Richard Stallman
Richard Stallman, born in 1953 in New York City to a Jewish family, developed an early interest in computers. After studying physics at Harvard and briefly pursuing a doctorate at MIT, he became an influential programmer at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. There, Stallman contributed to software projects such as TECO and Emacs, and challenged restricted computer access by promoting software freedom. His opposition to proprietary software and restrictive licensing, especially after experiences with inaccessible printer source code and companies like Symbolics, led him to initiate the GNU project in 1983 and found the Free Software Foundation (FSF). Stallman contributed essential tools like GNU Emacs, GCC, and GDB, and popularized the concept of copyleft through the GNU General Public License. He advocates for software users' freedoms to study, modify, and share software, emphasizing these as moral imperatives beyond practical benefits.
Stallman also campaigned against digital rights management, software patents, and surveillance, influencing movements and policies promoting free software. He insists on precise terminology, preferring "free software" over "open source" to highlight ethical values. After controversies related to comments on the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, Stallman resigned from MIT and the FSF presidency in 2019 but returned to the FSF board in 2021 amid divided community responses. Throughout his career, he has received numerous honors, including the MacArthur "genius grant," multiple honorary doctorates, and awards recognizing his foundational work in free software and programming.
